quest.title: Paimon's "Driyosh Problem-Solving Method"
quest.description: The first Adventurers' Tournament has concluded, with you and Paimon emerging as the winners. In addition to rewards from the Snezhnaya Headquarters, you'll also be faced with a series of special questions...

dialogues.speaker: Match Commentator
dialogues.text: To all the outstanding adventurers from across Teyvat — the first Adventurers' Tournament has officially come to an end.

dialogues.speaker: Match Commentator
dialogues.text: #The results are in, and the very title of "legend" has come to life: the unstoppable duo of {NICKNAME} and {M#his}{F#her} guide, Paimon, have claimed victory!

dialogues.speaker: Sukhrab
dialogues.text: This mysterious senior... is someone I'll definitely be striving toward in the future...

dialogues.speaker: Lan
dialogues.text: If it were anyone else knocking me out of first place at the very last moment, I might've been a little sore about it.

dialogues.speaker: Lan
dialogues.text: But if it's you and Paimon? Then what's there to say? That just makes it worth celebrating!

dialogues.speaker: Talalikhin
dialogues.text: Aside from the Mora reward, we've also prepared some commemorative items for you. Please wait a moment...

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Honestly, even though Paimon ended up joining this competition out of nowhere, and there weren't even that many spectators... well, it was a last-minute event, but Paimon still had a lot of fun!

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Besides, we also got some good practice in, and managed to sharpen those new skills we had just picked up!

response.speaker: Rika
response.text: Then what about the victory feast...?

response.speaker: Iris
response.text: We can talk about drinking later. The most important issue of this competition still hasn't been resolved.

response.speaker: Rika
response.text: Uh... Right. That's true.

response.speaker: Lan
response.text: Now that we have someone here who fully commands everyone's respect, the meeting we paused earlier should resume.

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: #According to the rules, when voting on any proposal, {NICKNAME}'s vote carries the same weight as everyone else combined.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Combined... meaning added together... so in other words...

response.speaker: Lan
response.text: #{NICKNAME} has a single vote that can approve or veto decisions outright, and can even suggest modifications directly.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: #So that's what it means to be the champion... At this point, anything {NICKNAME} says could influence hundreds or even thousands of adventurers.

choices.text: In that case, I'll have to think carefully about what I say now.

response.speaker: Urville
response.text: In short, logically speaking, the two of you are now effectively in charge of everyone here.

response.speaker: Liliuo
response.text: Alright, Boss! Meeting time — please hear our report!

response.speaker: Black Screen
response.text: During the long discussion, several decisive suggestions were made regarding key rules.

response.speaker: Black Screen
response.text:
The first pending rule turned into a chain of questions:
"Should full-time adventurers affiliated with the Guild have a required morning check-in time if they're not taking commissions outside the city?"
"If so, should it be 08:00 or 09:00?"
"What about the earliest possible off-duty time? How long should the lunch break be?"...
This single rule alone sparked a two-hour debate earlier.
Natlan and Sumeru representatives strongly opposed the idea, arguing that adventurers have highly irregular schedules — some operate at night, and may sleep through the entire day, even to the point where they can barely hold a sword properly due to reversed day-night cycles.

response.speaker: Black Screen
response.text: Fontaine and Inazuma, on the other hand, believed standardized management would improve Guild efficiency, and that adventurers could gradually adapt to healthier routines...\nAs for you and Paimon, considering you've never once reported to the Guild counter at a fixed time yourselves, you proposed a simple solution: Just set a latest check-in time each day.\nAll branches accepted this without objection. A problem that had remained unresolved for two hours was settled by you two in just ten minutes...

response.speaker: Black Screen
response.text:
Next came the key issue: "How should we quantify mission difficulty, introduce a rating system, and define the standards for commissions adventurers can take?"
And the related debate: "Should the system be strict to lower the overall average rating, or more lenient for flexibility?"
Under the preliminary design, once a difficulty rating system is introduced, commissions previously all classified as B-rank — such as those nicknamed "The Measure of a Mushroom" and "Emergency" — could differ by as much as 95 points in actual difficulty.
The downside is that using numerical difficulty instead of rank-based classification could prevent 30% to 50% of ordinary adventurers from accessing the latter half of commissions within the same rank, potentially reducing their income, discouraging participation, and harming the Guild's overall morale and potential.
The upside, however, is clear: safety comes first. With concrete numbers in front of them, fewer adventurers would overestimate their abilities and recklessly challenge powerful monsters. Injury rates would drop significantly, and medical costs would also be greatly reduced...

response.speaker: Black Screen
response.text:
The issue left both you and Paimon scratching your heads. It seemed like both sides had a point, so it was no wonder neither could convince the other.
In the end, Paimon cited a basic lesson that every Driyosh is expected to know, "the fundamental principles for conducting experiments on hypotheses involving unpredictable risks," and gave you a detailed explanation...
Drawing on those principles, you decided that each branch should first have its Intelligence Department compile and organize information gathered by ordinary adventurers. This would allow commissions to be evaluated more accurately and reduce errors caused by the current broad-brush rating system.

response.speaker: Black Screen
response.text: Next, a sufficiently large random sample of adventurers would be selected from the three participating branches and divided into six groups with evenly distributed strength and ranks for a six-month pilot program. The existing commission rank system and the new difficulty score system would then be applied to the groups respectively. Throughout the trial, the Guild would track metrics such as commission completion efficiency, injury rates, overall resource expenditure, and losses. The results would then be compared in detail, and the two systems evaluated comprehensively to determine which should be adopted. If necessary, different branches could even adopt different systems.\nImplementing this plan would require a tremendous amount of coordination and effort from every branch. The representatives present unanimously agreed and resolved to begin drafting their respective implementation plans as soon as the meeting concluded.

response.speaker: Black Screen
response.text: The remaining sixteen major rules were also revised based on you and Paimon's suggestions, and were ultimately finalized with broad consensus from all parties...

response.speaker: Urville
response.text: So, we've reached a conclusion on every agenda item, correct?

response.speaker: Liliuo
response.text: The rules I was most concerned about never sparked another argument. That's a good outcome, wouldn't you say?

response.speaker: Sarin
response.text: #Hmm, {NICKNAME} and Paimon's suggestions really hit the nail on the head...

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: At long last, our thorough and productive discussion has come to a close. We've reached a final consensus. Thank you all for your efforts.

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: Next, the staff at Headquarters will compile the finalized documents and send them to each of you for a final review. Before you leave, please remember to stop by and sign them.

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: As for the follow-up work, Headquarters will dispatch representatives to each branch at the appropriate time to assess implementation progress. We appreciate your full cooperation when the time comes.

response.speaker: Rika
response.text: No objections.

response.speaker: Lan
response.text: Same here.

response.speaker: Black Screen
response.text: The adventurers who attended the meeting bid you farewell one by one as the meeting adjourned.\nThe tense atmosphere lingering from the earlier disagreements had completely faded away...

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Phew... Paimon thought there'd be way more tricky stuff to deal with, but it actually wasn't so bad.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: At least there wasn't anything so serious that it'd make adventurers from one of the branches flip the table. Besides, the solutions in the handbook worked for just about everything.

choices.text: Hey, it wasn't exactly easy for me, either, you know?

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Really? Paimon made that big of a difference?

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Hehe, that's awesome! Paimon feels so proud!

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: For those of us at Headquarters, it's a good thing as well.

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: If you two hadn't been here today, I'm not sure how we would've wrapped things up.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Hmm... Then why go through all this trouble in the first place?

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: Hmm... Perhaps the more meaningful something is, the less easy it is to accomplish.

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: The Adventurers' Guild is an organization that spans all of Teyvat. At first glance, a long discussion filled with debate like today's might seem terribly time-consuming.

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: But if we don't take the time to listen to what members from every region truly care about, and instead impose rules on them without discussion...

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: An organization run that way would gradually lose the support of its members. It wouldn't last.

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: If we wait until problems arise before trying to resolve them, it may already be too late.

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: That's why we need both these discussions and the patience to see them through.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: As expected from someone at Headquarters... That was quite profound.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Well then, judging by the outcome, would you say we've gotten off to a good start?

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: A textbook-perfect start, if I do say so myself.

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: I won't lecture you any further. When you travel across different regions in the future, you'll see the results of this meeting for yourselves.

response.speaker: Talalikhin
response.text: It may not be anything grand, but it will surely bring a bit of your uniquely spirited energy to each branch.

choices.text: And everyone looked much more at ease when they left.
Without your help, I can't say how it would've turned out...
Let's take this seriously and go through the issues properly.
No need to be so formal.
